EXALGO(r) (HYDROMORPHONE HCI) EXTENDED-RELEASE TABLETS (CII) DELIVERS TRUE ONCE-DAILY DOSING WITH STEADY PLASMA LEVELS AROUND THE CLOCK.

* EXALGO reaches steady-state concentrations in 3 to 4 days, reducing peaks and troughs

At steady state, once-daily EXALGO provides a more stable and consistent concentration than IR hydromorphone.1,2
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_04.jpg]

Once-daily EXALGO is available in 8 mg, 12 mg, and 16 mg tablets that can be used in combination to achieve the desired
dosing strength; tablets should be swallowed whole.

INDICATION
EXALGO is an extended-release oral formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06m.jpg]

[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_07.jpg]


WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF
PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE

Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to respiratory depression.

Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only.
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental consumption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

Limitations of Use
EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain.
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic.
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.




[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08m.jpg]



*


EXALGO is also contraindicated in patients who:
- need management of mild pain or pain not expected
  to persist
- have significant impaired respiratory function including
  those with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia
- have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus
- have narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract
  including those from previous surgery or "blind loops"
  in the GI tract
- have known hypersensitivity to any components including
  hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites


*


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


*


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


*


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


*


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


*


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


*


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible
to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


*


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO

Subject: [RxNews] N Engl J Med    From 2010 through 2013,	there was a notable downturn in abuse of prescription opioids and a	coincident increase in abuse of heroin in the United States
From: Coolidge <coolidge@dakota2k.net>

To: NADDI <rxnews@listserve.com>


http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc1505541



Correspondence

Shifting Patterns of Prescription Opioid and Heroin Abuse in the United States

N Engl J Med 2015; 373:1789-1790October 29, 2015DOI: 10.1056/NEJMc1505541

Share:
{Facebook}
{Tweet}
{Google+}
{LinkedIn}




Article
To the Editor:

From 2010 through 2013, there was a notable downturn in abuse of prescription opioids and a coincident increase in abuse of heroin in the United States.1 Given that there is some evidence of a relationship between the two trends (e.g., some persons who abuse prescription opioids switch to heroin for a number of reasons and drug interchangeability has been observed),2-4 we sought to examine this relationship more closely, including the validity of reports suggesting regional differences in the balance between prescription opioid and heroin abuse.5

Data on opioid abuse in the previous month were collected quarterly from January 1, 2008, through September 31, 2014, with the use of self-administered surveys that were completed anonymously by independent cohorts of 15,227 patients with opioid dependence, as defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition, who were entering nonmethadone-maintenance treatment programs throughout the United States. Of these patients, 267 agreed to online interviews to gather qualitative information in order to amplify and interpret findings from the structured national survey.

Figure 1Figure 1National Rates of Abuse of Opioids in the Previous Month among 15,227 Respondents. shows the unadjusted rates of abuse of prescription opioids only, abuse of prescription opioids and heroin, or abuse of heroin only among respondents who reported such abuse in the previous month from 2008 through 2014. Rates of exclusive prescription opioid abuse remained stable from 2008 through 2010, at 70%, but then decreased steadily, with an average annual reduction of 6.1%, to less than 50% in 2014. Conversely, concurrent abuse of both heroin and prescription opioids in the previous month increased, with an average annual increase of 10.3%, from 23.6% in 2008 to 41.8% in 2014. Although the exclusive use of heroin was low in this population, it more than doubled from 2008 through 2014 (from 4.3% to 9.0%).

The national data obscure important regional differences (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, available with the full text of this letter at NEJM.org). The Northeast showed the most striking shifts in patterns of abuse. The West followed closely behind, with concurrent heroin and prescription opioid abuse surpassing exclusive prescription opioid abuse in 2014. The Midwest and South followed similar trends, with the latter showing exclusive prescription opioid abuse to be more prevalent than in any other region.

These findings suggest that as prescription opioid use has waned, concurrent heroin abuse has increased, with important, distinct regional variations. The factors contributing to these evolving changes are not well established. However, in our exploratory qualitative online survey of a subgroup of 267 patients, among the 129 respondents who reported abusing prescription opioids prior to heroin use, 73.0% (92 of 126 respondents) primarily cited practical factors, such as accessibility and cost, when explaining their transition to heroin. Three of the 129 respondents did not provide an explanation for their transition to heroin.


Theodore J. Cicero, Ph.D.
Matthew S. Ellis, M.P.E.
Jessie Harney, M.S.

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. - Florida has long been the nation's center of the illegal sale of prescription
drugs: Doctors here bought 89 percent of all the Oxycodone sold in the country last year. At its peak, so

many out-of-staters flocked to Florida to buy drugs at more than 1,000 pain clinics that the state earned

But with the help of tougher laws, officials have moved aggressively this year to shut down so-called
pill mills and disrupt the pipeline that moves the drugs north. In the past year, more than 400 clinics
were either shut down or closed their doors.
Prosecutors have indicted dozens of pill mill operators, and nearly 80 doctors have seen their licenses
suspended for prescribing mass quantities of pills without clear medical need.

MNKOI 0004418534

 New laws are also cutting off distribution. As of July, Florida doctors are barred, with a few
exceptions, from dispensing narcotics and addictive medicines in their offices or clinics. As a result,
doctors' purchases of Oxycodone, which reached 32.2 million doses in the first six months of 2010, fell
by 97 percent in the same period this year. The ban was phased in beginning last October, with a limit on
the number of pills a doctor could dispense.
"we had no tough laws in place; now we do," said Pam Bondi, Florida's attorney general.
Law enforcement agencies are also keeping a closer eye on pharmacies. The number of applications to open
new pharmacies in Florida has nearly doubled in the past two years, the result of doctors' facing tougher
rules. They now make up half of all the requests in the entire country, according to the latest Drug
Enforcement Administration figures.
Now, among other things, background checks are required for owners and employees. Violators, whether they
are pharmacists, doctors or clinic owners, face stiffer, swifter penalties if they prescribe or
distribute legal narcotic drugs to people who do not need them or without following required steps.
One indication that law enforcement officials are
choking<http://health.nytimes.com/health/guides/disease/acute-upper-airwayobstruction/overview.html?inline=nyt-classifier> the supply of prescription drugs sold illegally in
Florida is that the price of Oxycodone on the streets here has nearly doubled from last year, to $15 per
pill from $8, according to Capt. Eric Coleman, commander of the narcotics division of the Palm Beach
County Sheriff's Office. And on Commercial Boulevard, a major street in Broward County, the number of
pain clinics has fallen in the past year from 29 to one.
Treatment centers are also seeing more addicts seeking help. "We have patients walking in the door that
cannot afford prescription drugs any more," said Dr. Barbara Krantz, the chief executive and medical
director of Hanley Center, a large private treatment clinic in Palm Beach County.
Federal, state and local law enforcement officials have worked closely to increase the number of arrests
and major indictments. They are dealing with pill mill operators as they would large criminal
enterprises.
Last month federal prosecutors used racketeering laws to indict 32 people, including twin brothers who
they say operated a sprawling pill mill operation. The brothers, who owned four pain clinics, also were
charged with kidnapping, extortion and assault with a firearm under the indictment. Most of the
prescriptions<http://health.nytimes.com/health/guides/specialtopic/getting-a-prescriptionfilled/overview.html?inline=nyt-classifier> were written to patients who traveled to Florida from out of
state, with Kentucky making up the largest share.
And in a rare move, a Florida doctor who worked at one of the pain clinics was charged with murder by
Palm Beach County prosecutors after a patient died of an overdose in 2009, a few hours after the doctor
prescribed him 210 pain pills.
One of the brothers who owned the clinic, Jeffrey George, pleaded guilty<http://articles.sunsentinel.com/2011-08-29/health/fl-hk-jeff-george-pleads-guilty-20110829_1_pain-clinic-cynthia-cadetgeorge-twins> to second-degree murder this week. Prosecutors say the
twins<http://topics.nytimes.com/top/news/health/diseasesconditionsandhealthtopics/twins/index.html?inline
=nyt-classifier>' clinics were responsible for 56 overdose deaths.
The clinics were shut in 2010, but more than a year passed before the case was built, in part because
Oxycodone is legal and the new laws were not in place.
Charging a doctor and a clinic owner with homicide "was a game changer," said Sheriff Ric L. Bradshaw of
Palm Beach County. "You are not going to get a slap on the wrist. You are looking at life in prison."
Officials here acknowledge the drug problem is still alarming. Last year, seven people died in Florida
each day from prescription drug overdoses, a nearly 8 percent increase from 2009. This is far more than
the number who died from illegal drugs, and the figure is not expected to drop much this year. Oxycodone,
which when abused has an effect similar to heroin, was the most lethal.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=54A3B:B41DB4189704864061FB1363A448C720&> and Medication Guide<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=54A3C:B41DB4189704864061FB1363A448C720&>.

13:16 ET 6/20/11 [StreetAccount] PFE Preview of upcoming FDA decision on Pfizer/Pain Therapeutic's Remoxy (abuse-resistant formulation oxycodone) for moderate to severe pain ($20.20 -$0.06)

The PDUFA date for PFE/PTIE's class 2 NDA resubmission for Remoxy <https://www.streetaccount.com/biotech_search_productname.aspx?product_id=6018&searchtype=drug_names>  (extended release, abuse-resistant formulation oxycodone) for moderate to severe pain is 23-June. StreetAccount notes that the Street is generally expecting a delay to approval (Complete Response Letter) based on 3-May guidance provided by Pfizer. 

*	Background: 

	*	This FDA decision follows a December 2008 Complete Response Letter (CRL) and December 2010 resubmission, deemed a complete, class 2 filing in January. The CRL requested no new clinical trials, and sought additional non-clinical, later determined to be six-month stability data. The sponsor also took steps to strengthen the resubmission by completing a likeability study (positive topline results reported 25-Apr) and a pharmacokinetic trial in volunteers. 
	*	On May 16, 2011, the FDA met with members of the Industry Working Group (IWG) and other sponsors of Long Acting and Extended Release opioid drugs. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss the next steps in implementing A Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) for these products through a single shared system. 

		*	According to the FDA.gov website: "We continue to work on the Medication Guide Template and expect to be able to provide it by June 24, 2011." 

			*	StreetAccount notes that this is coincidentally one day after Pfizer's 23-Jun PDUFA date. 

*	Approval issues: 

	*	Recall that Pfizer warned, on its Q1 earnings call on May 3, that it was working to address a specific issue in the manufacturing section of the Remoxy application, as well as to understand any potential implications of FDA's recent class-wide REMS announcement for extended release opioids. Pfizer stated that these issues could delay the timing of approval or the launch of REMOXY. 

*	Leveraged: 

	*	Pfizer (PFE), via its $3.6B acquisition of King Pharmaceuticals, has worldwide commercialization rights, ex-Australia and New Zealand. 
	*	Pain Therapeutics (PTIE) is entitled to receive a 20% royalty except for the first $1B in cumulative net sales, which royalty is set at 15%; outside the US, the royalty rate is flat 10%. 
	*	Durect Corporation (DRRX) is entitled to a royalty of 6-11.5% of sales, paid by PFE and through PTIE supplemental to the royalty above, for the use of its Oradur technology. 

*	Competition: 

	*	Branded Extended Release Opioid Products listed by the FDA include JNJ's Duragesic and Exalgo (the latter with COV), ENDP's Opana ER, several privately-owned, as well as King Pharmaceuticals' (now part of Pfizer) Avinza and Embeda. 
	*	StreetAccount notes that ACUR/PFE's Oxecta (formerly Acurox), approved on 17-Jun, is an immediate release opioid (as opposed to extended release). 

*	Recent sell-side research, commentary: 

	*	BOAML noted on 16-May the Remoxy PDUFA as one of several potentially positive catalysts for shares for PFE. 
	*	UBS noted on 4-May that a "manufacturing delay seems likely", echoing management's remarks but notably more focused on the former warning versus the REMS-specific warning. 
	*	Wells Fargo noted on 3-May management's expectation for delay, due to the two issues mentioned above. 
	*	Goldman Sachs on 3-May projected revenues 2011-2016 of $22M, $85M, $228M, $358M, $441M and $475M. 
	*	Oppenheimer noted on 21-April in an ENDP note the potential approval of Remoxy as a competing drug to the Opana franchise. 
	*	Jefferies noted on 13-April in an ENDP note that Endo's Opana should be in "excellent shape with managed care (even with Remoxy entry)". 

Shares of PTIE are trading +4.1% to $8.99 ahead of the FDA decision, and in sympathy to Friday's FDA approval of ACUR's Oxecta, +24%.

Team Southern Heat,



I want to again thank each of you for your participation and attentiveness during our meeting in Miami this week.  Now that we have been back in the field a couple of days, I thought it would be useful to review some of the key points of the meeting and more importantly the direction going forward in Q2.  To sum it up simply, we need to be BALANCED, have FOCUS, and make calls with FREQUENCY.  Let's take a closer look at each of those:



*         BALANCE:

o    With 4 products in our bag, we need to "Balance" our time in the field very carefully.

o    We received our product weighting, and Exalgo remains our Flagship product in all territories throughout the district.

o    While Exalgo is key to our success, we can't maximize our IC plan, Contest dollars or sales force ranking without successfully promoting the NSAID basket and SDP.

o    The "Call Planner" will help you to balance your time and allocate your call capacity throughout the month. We will review this document together on each field visit. Don't wait to work on your Call Planner.  Each of you should have this complete and start to implement on Monday.  You can make changes throughout the quarter as needed.

*         FOCUS:

o    It is very important that we focus our time and resources on our most important customers who can provide the biggest return on our investment.

o    Plan "focused" dinner/lunch programs planned around hyper targets. You will get more out of this valuable resource.  Get those programs scheduled ASAP!!!

o    Focus your field time on the top decile physicians within each market basket.

o    Use IMS to identify top prescribing physicians who accept plans where our products are covered

o    Deliver a calculated message based upon a solid pre-call plan.  What are we going to say to move the customer during this call?  What are we going to ask for as a result of the interaction?

o    Use the new "Pre-Call Planning" document to help develop a goal for each call.

*         FREQUENCY:

o    Frequency of calls on your top prescribers/targets drives results!!!!

o    Our top prescribers should be seen at least once per week. (or at the very least 3 times per month)

o    When we are in the office 3+ times in a month, hyper targets prescribe twice the amount of EXALGO than when we are there 2 times/month.  This is evidence that your efforts make a difference!

o    Frequency with top targets in all three market baskets is key to our success. Market research shows that one call per month does nothing.



We cannot afford to waste any calls.  We need to challenge our customers' perceptions of hydromorphone, challenge them to identify a patient for EXALGO, challenge the coverage perceptions and how they are dosing EXALGO.  We need to sell with passion, enthusiasm, and confidence in all of our calls whether it's selling Exalgo, Sumavel DosePro, Pennsaid, and/or Duexis!!  Remember, these products can change patients' lives for the better!  We need to challenge our customers to ask their migraine patients......."How are you really doing?" Does their current therapy relieve all of their headache types? What about the wake up or the throw up headaches?  Sumavel DosePro can significantly help these patients.  We need to hypertarget our prescribers for Duexis and get those prescriptions written.  We need to maintain and increase our Pennsaid business by targeting managed care plans where we have the access via IMS and selling on our Simon data comparing Pennsaid to oral diclofenac.



Q2 will be a defining quarter for this business and for each of you.  We need to show what we are made of and put our mark on FY13 during this quarter and showing why we are designating ourselves as the Southern Heat.  Let's turn up the heat on ourselves and more importantly our customers to get the job done.  I am here to help each of you meet and exceed your goals.  We've been given the tools and the direction to be successful, it's now our job to implement and use them in the field!  Let's get to it!!!!





Great Selling!!!

CLEARWATER — A pain management doctor was arrested Monday evening on charges that she bought controlled substances by using fraudulent prescriptions.




According to the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office, Dr. Lynne C. Columbus filled the prescriptions at several pharmacies in Pinellas.

Deputies arrested her at her practice, Gulf Coast Pain Management, at 3001 Eastland Blvd. in unincorporated Clearwater.

The investigation began last month when detectives received a tip about Columbus writing prescriptions for oxycodone using patient's names.

Columbus, 50, faces charges of attempting to obtain controlled substances by fraud.

She was booked into the Pinellas County jail, but was released Monday night on $10,000 bail.

MNKOI 0003984687

 CVS refusing to fill some docs' pain pill scripts [The Orlando Sentinel , Fla.]

Dec. 01--CVS pharmacies in Florida will no longer fill the pain-pill
prescriptions written by certain doctors, the company confirmed this morning.
In a form letter sent to the affected physicians, the chain explained that it
will no longer fill their scripts for "schedule 2 narcotics", a class of pain
killer that includes oxycodone.
Those pills are at the heart of a lethal drug overdose epidemic in Florida. In
the first half of 2010, 1,268 people died here with at least one prescription
drug in their system that contributed to their deaths.
That's seven people a day.
In Orange and Osceola counties, the total for that same six-month period was
147.
Florida also has become a magnet for pain clinics. Ninety of the nation's top
100 oxycodone-buying doctors were in Florida last year, according to federal
records.
In June, there were an estimated 800 pain management clinics in Florida. Orange
County had 80.
Mike DeAngelis, CVS's head of public relations, today confirmed the new policy
at its Florida stores but would not provide details.
He would not say how many physicians are affected, other than to write in an
e-mail that it is "a small number".
The company sent the letters to doctors two weeks ago via Federal Express.
The drug store chain "has become increasingly concerned with escalating reports
of prescription drug abuse in Florida, especially oxycodone abuse," the letter
says.
DeAngelis would not say how the physicians were identified or why the ban comes
now but wrote, "We communicated with the DEA (Drug Enforcement Administration)
on this action."
Three months ago, in an effort to combat prescription abuse, the state
implemented a Prescription Drug Monitoring Program, a database that collects
information on who's using what and who's prescribing to whom.
It's designed to allow physicians to monitor what drugs their patients are
taking and where else they might be getting medication.

MNKOI 0003984688

 DeAngelis, the CVS spokesman, wrote, "CVS/pharmacy is unwavering in its
compliance and measures to prevent drug abuse and keep controlled substances out
of the wrong hands."
Oxycodone is often resold on the street and the target of thieves.
On back-to-back nights over the weekend, a man walked into separate Daytona
Beach drug stores, handed employees a note, implied that he was armed and
demanding oxycodone, police reported.
He got an undisclosed number of pills from a CVS on LPGA Boulevard, police
reported, but fled a walgreens empty-handed.

Subject: Medimpact presentation in San Diego today on Exalgo

 

Hi BJ,

 

Hope all is well.

 

Since you were not able to be there in person today, I wanted to give
you my perspective on the day. Overall take away: we are on to something
unique and innovative in this space.

 

First and foremost, all of what I am going to relate was made possible
by Bill's strong relationships in the account, meeting prep, logistical
execution and strategic account planning. As we both know, when all
these things are in place, the execution flows and we look good.

 

The presentation was in 4 basic parts:

 

1)     Bill nicely set it up, provided an overview of the agenda and
framed the approach we were about to take ( 5 min).

2)     Karrie provided a very succinct overview of Exalgo pharmacology
with appropriate emphasis on aspects relevant to this audience: e.g.
true QD, CYP insights, rationale for opioid rotation, dose dumping,
co-morbidities. Her presentation separated validity from relevance very
well. She handled questions with aplomb. ( about 25 mins)

3)     I presented the Exalgo REMS, the Exalgo REMS performance data,
and a CARES Alliance review. This was not REMSology 101, but an inside
view of REMS operations, and how we could work together to enhance
appropriate prescribing and safe use among their member prescribers and
patients. We also pitched some unique collaborative projects we can
discuss later.( 25 mins). Preston created a new deck and it is strong.

4)     Bill then did a crisp wrap-up and close.( 5 min)

 

There was one theme that Bill uncovered and briefed us on during  the
weeks leading to the meeting: Medimpact believes they have sufficient
opioids( LAO's and IR's) on their formulary to adequately treat pain,
and that adding another LAO will increase overall opioid use. To address
this Karrie emphasized that the rotation of tolerant patients does not
mean more opioid use, it promises better analgesia and/or fewer AEs.
That didactic element dovetailed nicely with all that we are doing in
the safe use area. Clearly, Exalgo and all that we offer with it, is a
solution, not part of the societal problem, and we are working to keep
it that way.

 

We had handouts and examples of many CARES tools, our posters on Tamper
Resistance and RxFMEA, and all were taken. When we mentioned we were
working with pain specialists like Joe Shurman, MD at Scripps San Diego,
and Mark Wallace, MD at UCSD we scored big. Bill's main contact wrote
these names down. I am sure he will check references.

 

It went well, and it can be even more focused and honed on customer
needs and concerns. I recommend we sit face to face and plan v2.0 off
this experience. Teamwork is a beautiful thing.

 

Leading the Science of Safety,

Art

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Arthur F. Morelli

Inflexxion is hosting this free 1-hour webinar on April 17 from 12 noon-1 PM CT (1-2 PM ET), and I m told that FDA representatives have registered for it.

 

I ve registered and will reserve Conference Room U (30 maximum) in the Learning Center (Building 10) for anyone who wishes to watch and listen   please bring your lunch.

 

For our Government Affairs and the MSLs, I suggest registering separately.

 

Feel free to share this invitation with others.

 

 

  

 
 

 New Strategies in Prescription Opioid Abuse Deterrence Measurement

Free Live Webinar:
April 17, 2014
1:00-2:00 pm EDT

The webinar will address some of the most pressing current issues pertaining to Abuse Deterrent Formulations (ADFs) of prescription opioids:

   How does the broader environment affect the likelihood that a given product will or will not demonstrate abuse deterrence?

   How to measure abuse deterrence when a product doesn't have a non-ADF precursor?

   What to do when measuring the abuse of a product with minimal or low market share?

These are some of the challenges that will be faced by manufacturers, regulators and public health authorities as new products are brought to market and seek ADF labeling.



 

{simonbudman}

  

  

 
Dr. Simon Budman, Moderator

  

 Theresa Cassidy, Presenter

  

 Dr. Edward Sellers, Discussant

 
A thought leader, researcher and innovator, Dr. Budman founded Inflexxion in 1989. He has lectured around the world and is an expert in data driven health quality improvement. Over the last 15 years, Dr. Budman has worked with most major companies in the prescription opioid area.

  

 Senior Director of Observational Epidemiology at Inflexxion. The Inflexxion team led by Ms. Cassidy and Dr. Stephen Butler has been working in the area of ADF and post-marketing studies for many years. They have advised numerous pharmaceutical clients, written peer reviewed papers, and presented to the FDA over an extended period.

  

 Dr. Sellers is an internationally recognized authority on clinical psychopharmacology, pharmacogenetics and smoking, abuse liability assessment and substance abuse. He has worked as an independent consultant with academic institutions, hospitals, government agencies, investors and biopharmaceutical and device companies achieving a deep understanding of their needs.

 


This webinar will be an opportunity to learn more about how the Inflexxion team is addressing the challenges of ADF measurement. We will welcome your questions and comments at the webinar.

Let’s step back here.

 

Bruce is working the ASR for single sided H transactions where the registration number is improperly captured.

 

The ARCOS reporting is likely taking the data straight from the very files which have the bad data as a result of this issue.

 

Once this issue is resolved, the ARCOS reports can be run to verify the correct registration number appears. If this is still an issue, a new ASR can be kicked off.

 

On a side note, there is a State ARCOS report ASR that is in progress. Not sure how this is related.

Todd

Subject: RE: ARCOS



 

The ASR I am testing with Carrie is the only ARCOS ASR I am aware of.  I cannot initiate ASRs.

Sent: Thursday, July 08, 2010 5:11 PM
To: Spaulding, Eileen L.
Cc: Bruce Barker; Johnson, Carrie M
Subject: RE: ARCOS



 

Eileen,

 

I don’t remember an ASR being started.  I asked Bruce to send you the current ASR information, but we were waiting for the DEA Annual ASR to finish (it is being tested now). 

 

St. Louis was in the middle of the work stoppage, so I asked you to submit the ASR.  I doubt if we can get anything done before the 15th.  With ARCOS there is no QA version of HDDLIB, so the testing has to be done in Dilbert (which we don’t have access to).  This extends the testing another week or more because of communication issues.

 

Bruce,

Do you have an ASR for single sided H transactions in ARCOS?  Can you initiate one using the same information and test data as the one you are finishing up now?

 

Sincerely,

Lee Nelson
(314) 654-1565  lee.nelson@covidien.com


 

From: Spaulding, Eileen L.
Sent: Thursday, July 08, 2010 14:55
To: Nelson, Lee
Subject: FW: ARCOS



 

Lee,

 

How do we stand on the ASR to fix the ARCOS system that has this same problem.  I see the progress being done on the DEA database with the registration numbers.

 

I know we discussed this on one of our all-site conference calls, but cannot positively recall the outcome and I can't find an e-mail about it.  We're you going to submit an ASR for the ARCOS system or were we waiting to see if the current ASR will fix both the ARCOS and the DEA systems at the same time?

 

I have a whole bunch of errors to correct for 1st quarter and I am trying not to generate as many errors for the 2nd quarter.

 

Thank you,

 


Eileen

 


 


-----


From: Nelson, Lee
Sent: Wednesday, April 21, 2010 10:48 AM
To: Spaulding, Eileen L.; Lewis, Mary
Cc: Johnson, Carrie M
Subject: RE: ARCOS

Eileen,

 

Yes, this is a known problem in BPCS.  BPCS switched from the U transaction to the H transaction to receive inter-company shipments.  However the single sided H transaction has never worked in ARCOS or DEA Annual. 

 

ASR516327 - BPCS-ST/HB-(ASR MFG00605) Re-supply order receipts not picking up correct DEA registration (Bruce Barker)

 

This ASR was for the DEA system only.  I asked about ARCOS, but they said that would need a separate ASR (it has not been submitted).

 

The fix is to create separate Hobart customer numbers for each inter-company H transaction, then enter vendor information on that customer number.

St. Louis manufacturer à Hobart (new Hobart number with St. Louis manufacturer registration)

St. Louis distributor à Hobart (new Hobart number with vendor registration)

Webster manufacturer à Hobart  (new Hobart number with vendor registration)

Webster researcher à Hobart  (new Hobart number with vendor registration)

Etc.

Then copy the B transaction look-ups into the H transaction code (customer registration will now be associate registration).

 

Sincerely,

Lee Nelson
(314) 654-1565  lee.nelson@covidien.com


 

From: Spaulding, Eileen L.
Sent: Wednesday, April 21, 2010 08:46
To: Nelson, Lee; Lewis, Mary
Subject: ARCOS



 

Lee/Mary,


 


I received my 1st Qtr ARCOS error report back and I receive an error for every Putup and Fentanyl Lozenge shipment from STLP to Hobart.  The system is pulling in my DEA Reg# RM0270037 as the purchased from DEA Reg# instead of your Mfg DEA Reg# PM0037451.  Is this something in the system or is it possible that when the order is being created the wrong DEA Reg# is being keyed into the field?


 


I remember something about an ASR for a similar problem to this, but I am unsure if it was completed or not.


 


You should be okay on your side because it will record a "S" transaction to my registration, but all my "P" transactions are also registering my registration and it appears that I am buying the material from myself.


 


Any light you can shed would be appreciated.


 


Regards,


 


Eileen L. Spaulding

Stratify Patients for Opioid Misuse and Abuse Risk
By: ALICIA AULT, Family Practice News Digital Network<mailto:a.ault@elsevier.com>
12/05/11
________________________________
FROM THE AMERICAN MEDICAL ASSOCIATION HOUSE OF DELEGATES INTERIM MEETING
________________________________
NEW ORLEANS - Do you know which of your patients is likely to misuse or abuse opioid medications?
They can be stratified according to risk, but many physicians don't know how or don't take the time to do so, according to Dr. Lynn R. Webster, medical director of Lifetree Clinical Research in Salt Lake City and director at large for the American Academy of Pain Medicine.
It is important to try to prevent misuse or abuse, given that overdoses and deaths from prescription drugs are on the rise, said Dr. Webster at the American Medical Association House of Delegates Interim meeting.
According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse<http://www.nida.nih.gov/infofacts/hospitalvisits.html>, emergency department visits involving nonmedical use of pharmaceuticals (either alone or in combination with another drug) increased 98% between 2004 and 2009, from 627,291 visits to 1.2 million visits. There was an 83% rise in emergency department visits involving adverse reactions to pharmaceuticals between 2005 and 2009, from 1.3 million to 2.3 million visits.
Opioids were the most frequently cited in those ED visits, accounting for about 50% of nonmedical use. Psychotherapeutic agents accounted for a third of the nonmedical use. According to the National Institute on Drug Abuse, the three most frequently cited drugs in those visits were hydrocodone (alone or in combination), accounting for 104,490 visits; oxycodone (alone or in combination), for 175,949 visits; and methadone, for 70,637 visits.
To properly assess and treat patients, physicians should understand and agree upon terminology, said Dr. Webster. Patients may "misuse" prescriptions if they are not taking them as directed. They aren't seeking a high, they may just have undertreated pain, he said.
Abuse is the willful self-administration of a drug to get high. Addiction is a medical condition with complex genetic, psychosocial, and environmental factors that influence its development and manifestations. Addicts may have impaired control over drug use, compulsive use, or continued use despite harm.
"You don't just put someone on an opioid and think you've done your job."
Pseudoaddiction results from undertreatment of pain, and may resolve with proper therapy. Patients in this state may manifest behavior that is misidentified as drug-seeking, according to Dr. Webster.
Even with chronic pain, "people prescribed opioids over a long period of time are going to have aberrant behavior," said Dr. Webster, noting that "it's not a small problem." In research he conducted, up to 40% of patients in his chronic pain practice had aberrant behavior within a year of starting treatment.
But, he said, "only a small percent have the disease of addiction."
To prevent misuse and abuse, it's important to understand patients' motives, he said. Nonmedical users may have been prescribed pain medications, but they move on to recreational use and then, often, abuse.
Medical users generally are pain patients who are seeking more pain relief and end up misusing the drugs. They also may become abusers. In all, 40%-60% have other chronic conditions for which opioids provide relief, such as anxiety, said Dr. Webster. That use is obviously not appropriate, but it can only be prevented if physicians fully assess pain patients.
There is a constellation of risk factors that help determine potential for misuse and abuse, according to Dr. Webster.
The potency of a pharmacologic substance and how fast it works are important, as those factors help determine how much dopamine is released, and thus, the amount of reward the patient feels, said Dr. Webster. If the drug is readily available, that also determines its attractiveness.
One-fifth of the overall population is at risk for addiction. There is no on/off switch, but a continuum of risk, he explained. Biological, psychiatric, and social factors all play a role in where patients fall on that continuum. Age, gender, family history, cigarette smoking, pain severity and duration, and sleep disorders are all risk factors. Patients with a history of a psychiatric disorder, being sexual abused, or substance use disorder also are at higher risk. "We must assess mental health," said Dr. Webster, noting that patients with anxiety, depression, traumatic brain injury, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder are at risk for self-medicating and overdose.
A history of legal problems and motor vehicle accidents, or poor family support and unemployment also are predictors, Dr. Webster said.
Aberrant behaviors are directly related to the duration and the intensity of pain. Patients who cannot completely eliminate their pain may resort to taking more medication, which they will see as less of a wrong than the pain itself, he said.
Physicians generally have not done a good job at evaluating these risks, and selecting and managing patients according to these factors. But how patients are managed can help determine whether they end up in the emergency room, "or going to a substance abuse treatment center or the morgue," he said.
There are tools that can be used to screen patients for risk. Among those are the Screener and Opioid Assessment for Patients With Pain (SOAPP); the Opioid Risk Tool (ORT); the Diagnosis, Intractability, Risk Efficacy (DIRE) test; and the Current Opioid Misuse Measure (COMM), which is used for patients already taking opioids.

[http://www.familypracticenews.com/uploads/RTEmagicC_2bh694wv_85390.graphic.im.jpg.jpg]

These tests all are simple and take only 1 to 10 minutes to administer. They can be given by any physician, including primary care physicians, he said.
Once all the factors are taken into account, patients can be stratified according to risk. Lower-risk patients - those with moderate pain and no personal or family history of substance use disorders - can be managed by primary care physicians. Those at moderate risk may need the addition of a pain specialist. The higher-risk patients will need consultations with mental health professionals and pain physicians.
Monitoring higher-risk patients may require urine drug testing and prescription monitoring programs. Pharmacists should be kept in the loop to see whether patients are shopping around. Family and friends can be invaluable sources to help identify risky behaviors.
Physicians need to do a better job of titrating opioids and determining proper dosing. Many patients have died at initiation of opioid therapy, or from rotating from one drug to another, he said. Patients should not be allowed to determine how much of a long-acting medication they can take.
So how do doctors mitigate risk? The first order of business is to treat the pain. "Uncontrolled pain, untreated pain, I believe is the number one reason for aberrant behavior," said Dr. Webster. Physicians cannot eliminate all pain, however, so education also is crucial.
Physicians also have a duty to monitor pain patients. "You don't just put someone on an opioid and think you've done your job," said Dr. Webster. A doctor would not stop managing a diabetic; pain patients need long-term management, he said.
Dr. Webster reported having no relevant conflicts of interest.

A raid on a medical clinic in Panorama City yesterday resulted in 70 arrests, including of physicians,
for allegedly operating an illegal Oxycontin prescription ring or "pill mill ."
Wednesday morning's raid on the Roscoe Van Nuys Medical Clinic included the arrest of Dr. Manuel Sison,
the clinic's medical director, who is also a physician at the L.A. County Jail, CBS
reports<http://losangeles.cbslocal.com/2012/05/09/agents-raid-doctors-van-nuys-office-in-allegedprescription-drug-ring/>.
During the raid, authorities from county, state and federal agencies found 42 patients in the clinic -more than the clinic plausibly could have been taking on for legitimate medical concerns, agents told
CBS.
According to wire service reports<http://northridge.patch.com/articles/northridge-woman-among-70arrested-in-pill-mill-raids#photo-9882148>, the clinic at 8121 Van Nuys Blvd. was raided by the Health
Authority Law Enforcement Taskforce, or HALT, consisting of authorities from the FBI, the L.A. County
Sheriff's Department, the state Department of Justice, the DEA, the IRS and the county Department of
Health and Human Services. A description of the task force<http://lasheriff.org/divisions/detective/major_crimes/mjrcrm.html> by the Sheriff's Department says that it
"investigates Medi-Cal fraud, counterfeit and illegal distribution of pharmaceuticals and the illegal
practice of medicine and dentistry."
Also arrested among the doctors, patients and clinic staff was the clinic's manager, 52-year-old Aida
Hawatmeh of Northridge. Several other doctors and clinic staff remain under investigation in the case,
authorities said.
A "pill mill" is a place where drug dealers and addicts can pay hundreds of dollars for prescriptions -usually for the powerful narcotic painkiller

 Oxycontin/Oxycodone<http://drpullen.com/oxycontinvsoxycodone> -- without ever being examined by a doctor.
The illegal operations can pull down many thousands of dollars a day. Authorities said Roscoe Van Nuys
Medical Clinic was shut down once before for operating as a pill mill, but reopened later under different
doctors.

Please join us for an important event!

 
THURSDAY, OCTOBER 18, 2012
Two Live Broadcasts
7:30 PM EST | 9:30 PM EST

 
 

You are invited to participate in the upcoming National
Broadcast Event "Important Considerations in Customizing
Pain Management: Patient Selection and Dosing Strategies."
The expert faculty panel will cover the following information:

 

 Establish a rationale for choosing a long-acting
extended-release opioid

 
 

 Define proper patient selection

 
 

 Explore dosing conversion and titration strategies

 
 

 Improve prescriber-patient communication to help
facilitate successful treatment outcomes

 

PROGRAM DETAILS



 See the Program Chair, Michael Brennan, MD, describe the importance of this educational event.

 


 
Important: At the conclusion of the video, you will be
directed to the Registration website. If you are in the
Eastern or Central time zones please use NEbroadcast for
your invitation code. If you live in the Mountain or Pacific time zones, please use WTbroadcast for your invitation code.
If you are unable to make it to a meeting site, you also can
view the event from your home computer.

 

This interactive program will be broadcast to 60 venues
throughout the United States on Thursday, October 18th,
and will include a complimentary dinner at each venue.
The first live broadcast begins at 7:30 PM EST; a second live
broadcast will begin at 9:30 PM EST.

SEATING IS LIMITED REGISTER TODAY!

RSVP today using one of the following methods:

1.

 Online at: www.HLXBroadcast.com. If you are in the

your invitation code. If you live in the Mountain or Pacific
time zones, please use WTbroadcast for your invitation code.

 
2.

 Call: 800-111-0467.

 
3.

 Contact your Mallinckrodt sales representative for more
information.

 

This event is promotional; there are no certified continuing medical education credits approved for this presentation. Covidien proudly adheres to the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers Association Code for Interactions with Healthcare Professionals. Attendance must be limited strictly to healthcare professionals. Spouses and other guests cannot be accommodated. Thank You.

Expert Faculty Panel

Michael Brennan, MD (Program Chair)
The Pain Center of Fairfield
Fairfield, CT

Charles E. Argoff, MD, PhD
Albany Medical College
Albany Medical Center
Albany, NY

Joseph Shurman, MD
Scripps Memorial Hospital
San Diego, CA

In addition to a live Question and Answer session with the
nationally recognized faculty, there will be robust post-event discussion at each venue led by a local faculty speaker.

 


800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally registered trademarks of Covidien AG. EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20185 October 2012

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase.
Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

Orange Park 'Pill Mill' Doctors Arrested
POSTED: Wednesday, May 11, 2011

Adla Adi and Terry Howard

Booking photos of
Adla Adi and Terry Howard

CONFIDENTIAL

MAL-MI 000116509

 ORANGE PARK, Fla. -- Two doctors were arrested Wednesday and charged in connection to the investigation of Total Medical
Express, an Orange Park that the Clay County Sheriff's Office calls a "pill mill."
The business was raided in March 2011 on suspicion of prescription fraud and operating an unregistered pain clinic. Several
customers and the office manager were arrested then on various charges.
Adla Adi, 72, of Ponte Vedra, turned himself in on charges of owning or operating an nonregistered pain management clinic.
Terry Howard, 58, was picked up by U.S. marshals in Orlando on the Clay County warrant.
According to the arrest warrant, Adi and Howard admitted to being the only doctors who saw patients during certain days at the
business, and the only ones in the business on those days authorized to write prescriptions.
Investigators said the business was attracting drug dealers and users from across the region.
"Prescription fraud is quickly becoming the scourge of many communities and our goal is to stop its impact on Clay County by
holding accountable the doctors who are the very source of the problem," said Clay County Sheriff Rick Beseler. "Not only did
we arrest the customers of the 'pill mill,' but now also the doctors themselves. Arrests made at the physician level are a rare and
important step for local law enforcement."
Adi posted $250,003 bond and was released. Howard is being held in a correctional facility in Seminole County and is scheduled
to appear before a judge on the Clay County charge on Thursday.

This coverage is not sanctioned by, nor a part of, the American Association of Pain Management.

Extended-Release Hydromorphone Shows Safety, Efficacy for Sustained Pain Control
Nancy A. Melville
October 22, 2009 (Phoenix, Arizona)   An extended-release form of the opioid drug hydromorphone (Exalgo, Neuromed Pharmaceuticals) provides effective and safe therapy for chronic moderate to severe lower back pain, according to a phase 3 study presented here at the American Association of Pain Management 20th annual clinical meeting.
Although similar in efficacy to the opioid morphine, hydromorphone offers an advantage in the treatment of pain in the elderly and patients with problems with renal clearance of drugs because it lacks the active metabolites that are present in morphine, said Douglas Gourlay, MD, director of the Pain and Chemical Dependency Division, Wasser Pain Centre, Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto, Ontario.
"Morphine is often considered a poor choice for the elderly or people who are renally impaired because of the active metabolites, but hydromorphone offers an advantage, in that it's a relatively clean molecule, so it's often preferred," said Dr. Gourlay, who was not involved in the study. "It's a potent opioid with nice, clean kinetics."
The double-blind study involved 268 patients with mild to severe lower back pain who were randomized into 2 groups of 134 patients each to receive either extended release hydromorphone or placebo for 12 weeks. The patients recorded pain intensity scores on an 11-point Likert Numeric Rating Scale. Results were presented at the meeting by Arifulla Khan, MD, medical director and principal investigator of Northwest Clinical Research Center in Bellevue, Washington.
The results showed significant improvements in changes in mean pain intensity scores from baseline to week 12 between the hydromorphone group (median, 0.2) and the placebo group (median, 1.6; P < .0001).
Adverse events reported by the hydromorphone group were similar to those of other oral opioids, including drug withdrawal syndrome (7.5%), constipation (6%), nausea (3%), and headache (3%).
An extended-release hydromorphone product made its way to the American marketplace briefly under the name Palladone, but the product was voluntarily withdrawn in 2005 by maker Purdue Pharma after a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory issued a warning of potentially fatal adverse effects related to dose dumping when combined with alcohol.
Joanna Schooler, a spokesperson for Neuromed, said that data provided to the FDA indicate that Exalgo is not subject to dose dumping.
"In vitro studies have shown that alcohol in various concentrations does not alter the extended-release properties or pharmacokinetic profile of Exalgo," she said.
The benefits of a controlled-release formulation of hydromorphone are 2-fold; it offers improved steady pain control and serves as a deterrent for abuse, Dr. Gourlay noted.
"There is clearly a population of patients who struggle with withdrawal-mediated pain resulting from the waxing and waning of drug levels from medication taken over the course of a 24-hour period, and the ultimate effect is that their pain is amplified," he said.
"The idea with the controlled release is to not only reduce the tendency toward multiple doses required throughout the day, but also to give increased stability and have a lower incidence of that withdrawal-mediated pain."
The steady delivery of the drug also eliminates the highs and lows that make the drug susceptible to abuse.
"Drugs that rapidly cross over the blood brain barrier and that peak quickly and fall off quickly tend to be drugs with higher abuse liability, so the theoretical advantage of a controlled-release delivery system is that the reward associated with taking the drug is less intense and will hopefully have a lower abuse liability," he said.
The study received funding from Neuromed Pharmaceuticals. Dr. Gourlay has disclosed no relevant financial relationships.
American Association of Pain Management (AAPM) 20th annual clinical meeting: Poster abstract 2. Presented October 9, 2009.

In This Issue

Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 Introduced

Reps. Bob Latta (R-Ohio) and Jim Matheson (D-Utah) introduced the Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 (H.R. 1919) on May 9. The bill reflects the legislative discussion draft on pharmaceutical supply chain safety and traceability that was marked up May 7 by the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health. During the markup, legislators discussed wholesaler licensure standards, federal preemption of state pedigree laws, returns processing and verification and the migration to unit-level serialization and traceability. Members on both sides of the aisle urged bipartisan cooperation and supported the process moving forward with patience and collaboration.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee scheduled a full committee markup of H.R. 1919 for May 14 at 4:00 p.m. in room 2123 of the Rayburn House Office Building, which will continue into a legislative markup on May 15 at 10:00 a.m. Additional details are available through the committee website.

For more information, contact Liz Gallenagh.
{top of page}

Legislators Send Letter to FDA on Hydrocodone-Combination Product Rescheduling

Senators Mark Kirk (R-Ill.), Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) and a bipartisan, bicameral group of legislators sent a March 9 letter to FDA Commissioner Margaret Hamburg urging the agency to take action on rescheduling hydrocodone combination products. This letter is a follow up to one sent earlier this year imploring the FDA to act quickly on the FDA Advisory Committee's recommendation.

In addition to Senators Kirk and Manchin, the letter also was signed by Senators Jay Rockefeller (D-W.Va.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Bill Nelson (D-Fla), Marco Rubio (R-Fla) and Representative Vern Buchanan (R-Fla).

Additional details, including the text of the letter, are available in the press release.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.
{top of page}

California Board of Pharmacy Establishes E-Pedigree Committee, Announces June Meeting

The California Board of Pharmacy established a separate E-Pedigree Committee, which will focus solely on matters pertaining to the implementation of California's e-pedigree law. The next meeting is set for June 24 in Sacramento. An agenda will be released 10 days prior to the meeting.

For more information, contact Liz Gallenagh.
{top of page}

Florida DWDAC to Hold Conference Call

The Florida Drug Wholesale Advisory Council (DWDAC) is hosting a conference call on May 16 at 9:30 a.m. (EDT). The agenda and meeting materials will be posted prior to the call and may be accessed here. The DWDAC provides input to the Division of Drugs, Devices and Cosmetics.

For more information, contact Dan Bellingham.
{top of page}

Original Formulation of Opana ER Can Stay on Market — FDA

On May 10, FDA responded to a petition filed by Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc., and concluded that the original formulation of Opana ER (oxymorphone hydrochloride) Extended-Release Tablets should not be be withdrawn from the market for reasons of safety or effectiveness. For further information, see the FDA website.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.
{top of page}

DEA Hosting Manufacturer/Importer/Exporter Conference

DEA is hosting a national two-day Manufacturer/Importer/Exporter Conference on Tuesday, June 18 and Wednesday, June 19 in National Harbor, Md. The conference will present federal laws and regulations that affect the pharmaceutical and chemical manufacturing, importing, and exporting industry and tiscuss practices to prevent diversion while minimizing the impact on legitimate commerce. In addition, topics such as quotas, year-end reporting, ARCOS reporting, import/export permits and declarations will be discussed.

Registration is available on a first-come, first-served basis. Further information, including an agenda and a registration form, can be found on the DEA website.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca.

FDA approves abuse-deterrent labeling for reformulated OxyContin
Agency will not approve generics to original OxyContin
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved updated labeling for Purdue Pharma L.P.'s
reformulated OxyContin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) tablets. The new labeling indicates
that the product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection
difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting).
Additionally, because original OxyContin provides the same therapeutic benefits as reformulated
OxyContin, but poses an increased potential for certain types of abuse, the FDA has determined that the
benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks and that original OxyContin was withdrawn
from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. Accordingly, the agency will not accept or approve any
abbreviated new drug applications (generics) that rely upon the approval of original OxyContin.
The FDA approved the original formulation of OxyContin in Dec. 1995. The product was abused, often
following manipulation intended to defeat its extended -release properties. Such manipulation causes the
drug to be released more rapidly, which increases the risk of serious adverse events, including overdose
and death. In April 2010, the FDA approved a reformulated version of OxyContin, which was designed to be
more difficult to manipulate for purposes of misuse or abuse. Purdue stopped shipping original OxyContin
to pharmacies in August 2010.
"The development of abuse-deterrent opioid analgesics is a public health priority for the FDA," said
Douglas Throckmorton, M.D., deputy director for regulatory programs in the FDA's Center for Drug
Evaluation and Research. "While both original and reformulated OxyContin are subject to abuse and misuse,
the FDA has determined that reformulated OxyContin can be expected to make abuse by injection difficult
and expected to reduce abuse by snorting compared to original OxyContin."
The FDA has determined that the reformulated product has abuse-deterrent properties. The tablet is more
difficult to crush, break, or dissolve. It also forms a viscous hydrogel and cannot be easily prepared
for injection. The agency has determined that the physical and chemical properties of the reformulated
product are expected to make the product difficult to inject and to reduce abuse via snorting. However,
abuse of OxyContin by these routes, as well as the oral route, is still possible. The reformulated
product also may reduce incidents of therapeutic misuse, such as crushing the product to sprinkle it onto
food or to administer it through a gastric tube. When FDA finds that a new formulation has abuse
deterrent properties, the agency has the authority to require generics to have abuse-deterrent properties
also
The agency review of this issue included an analysis of the following:

MNKOI 0000602185

 Citizen petitions requesting that the agency determine whether original oxyContin was
voluntarily withdrawn from sale for reasons other than safety or effectiveness;
comments submitted to the public dockets associated with these petitions;
Information concerning original and reformulated oxyContin and the withdrawal of original
oxyContin;
clinical data, peer-reviewed literature, and other information concerning postmarketing adverse
events associated with original oxyContin, reformulated oxyContin, and other extended -release oxycodone
products.
Postmarketing assessments of the impact of reformulated oxyContin on abuse are ongoing, and the FDA will
update its evaluation of the effects of reformulated oxyContin on abuse as new data become available.
The FDA, together with other public health agencies, continues to encourage the development of abusedeterrent formulations of opioids and believes that such products will help reduce prescription drug
abuse. At the same time, the FDA remains committed to ensuring that patients with pain have appropriate
access to °plaid analgesics.

March 28, 2014

By HEALTH NEWS FLORIDA STAFF

On both Florida coasts, the toll of oxycodone continues, as a doctor is arrested and clinic owners are convicted.

 

The Boca Raton Police arrested Dr. Harry Kesten, 47, owner of Quick Test Labs in Delray Beach, after he tried to buy $300 worth of oxycodone pills, the South Florida Sun Sentinel reports. Police used an undercover informant to tape a phone conversation, then set up the fake buy.

 

In the recorded call, according to the arrest report, Kesten said he could falsify drug test results and make fake labels for prescription bottles.

 

Meanwhile in Tampa, in a case that took years to bring to trial, a jury convicted the operators of First Medical Group pain clinic of trafficking in oxycodone as well as conspiracy, the Tampa Bay Times reports.

 

Those who were convicted after five days of jury deliberation were clinic owners Jorge Gonzalez-Betancourt, 53, and Michele Gonzalez, 37, both of Tampa, and manager was Maureen Altman, 58, of Lakeland.

 

The clinic's physician, Dr. Kimberly Daffern, died in 2011 before the case went to trial. As the Times reports, he was accused of prescribing 1 million oxycodone pills in three months.

 

Even though the clinic attracted hordes of customers from as far as Ohio and Kentucky, it took years of investigation for years before prosecutors felt there was enough evidence to go to trial.

 

It is notoriously difficult to prosecute drug cases involving prescription drugs. Last month, the three-month-long trial of a Palm Beach County physician and pharmacist ended in acquittal. Dr. Timothy Sigman and pharmacist Peter Del Toro had been charged with dealing in human growth hormone, testosterone and anabolic steroids.
