Cc: Gunn, Edward <EGunn@gsw-w.com>
Sent: Thu Nov 11 10:52:57 2010
Subject: 1st Interview
Good Morning!  Just wanted to give you a little feedback from our first interview.  I captured their initial reactions to the concepts, quotes, etc. below.  Showing the sales aid first seems to be working well and this doctor got every concept pretty amazing.   Will keep you updated.

 

Respondent #1  (Rank:  Pitfalls, Good Day, Challenges)

 

Doctor not familiar with EXALGO at all.

 

Pitfalls

SA:  Sees it as a bomb on the front cover.  Informs him of the 24 hour benefit overall.  "It's a ticking time bomb going down and the inside is a pill with a timer representing of the technology built into the pill."

Ad1/2:  "As the day wears on and the person does the stuff they need to do, there is a chance without 24 hour relief, there might be problems in activities." 

Overall:  All about activity of daily living and being able to continue on without having to stop.  Seeing the adlobs helps him to lock in the idea of daily activity help for 24 hours, when paired with the sales aid.  This is talking about extended, 24 hour relief.

 

Challenges (5): 

SA/Adlobs:  Idea is it is a challenge to do a lot of activities for a patient.  Using a medication to overcome that challenge is the message.  

Overall:  I don't get the 24 hour relief message right away.  I get the challenge of going to the mailbox and the office.

 

Good Day  (5-"I like the idea of being able to go through good and bad days without the extra burden of pain problems"):

SA-A busy person that has a filled schedule of doing unpleasant things.  This can be a good day, even though it's a bad day because they don't have other relief issues.  It doesn't talk about the chronic pain much, so it could be confusing why it's a good day (just only having seen the Sales Aid without the adlob imagery).

Adlobs:  "It's saying, you can make a good thing out of bad situations.  This is a concept of something unpleasant and someone having fun out of it, making good out of bad.  The concept is a little "over the top", I have never had a tornado at a picnic and not run, and you might think someone was a little crazy for this.  The cartoon display is fine and it could seem too realistic if not in cartoon form.

Overall:  With the unpleasantness of the overall day, it can still be a good day. "this is correct, they will get 24 hour relief with this medication and can spend time with the mother-in-law".

Subject:
Thank you and follow-up on C.A.R.E.S. Alliance Fall Summit
Attachments: Fall Summit Survey_FINAL_11.3.11.doc

Sent on behalf of Dr. Herb Neuman and Art Morelli

Dear Paul,
Thank you for joining us at the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance Fall Summit and for participating in the robust, action-oriented discussion.
The purpose of the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance is to reduce prescription drug abuse and misuse through collaboration — and the
conversation and action items that came out of the Summit will help to guide our collective efforts moving forward. Below are
a few potential opportunities discussed at the Summit:
•

•
•

The AAPM prescriber education event at the end of February in Palm Springs. This will include an innovative and
practical PCP-targeted education session on opioids and PMPs, a state-of-the-art drug take-back event and associated
patient education kiosks, media, etc. Several organizations — Project Lazarus, American Pain Foundation, American
Chronic Pain Foundation, in particular — expressed an interest in helping AAPM and the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance see this
through.
The Partnership at Drugfree.org's strong proposal on educating parents and their children via a proven media
approach.
Take-back days as standalone or embedded opportunities that continue to promote safe use and prevent abuse and
misuse.

This is just the beginning and we hope all attending organizations will get involved in the collaborative spirit. If you have
additional thoughts that did not get shared yesterday, we'd love to hear from you right away.
We will also be sharing full details on the Fall Summit with organizations that were not able to attend to increase awareness
and participation beyond those who were at the meeting.
As we discussed at the Summit, there is a need for increased communication to enable planning and enhance awareness of
what the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance is doing and also what all the participant organizations are doing. In the coming days, you will
receive further post-Summit communications from us with full notes from the day and an action plan for next steps. We
would like to share the master deck of everyone's presentations as well as all attendees' email addresses, please let us know
by early next week if you do not want us to share either of these pieces of information. Over the coming months we will be
communicating with you more regularly. Please share with us any activities or initiatives that you would like us to distribute to
all the participants in the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance.
For those who did not complete the survey distributed at the end of the Summit, it is attached to this email. Your feedback is
important, as it informs future Summits. Thank you in advance for taking the time to reply.
On behalf of the entire Covidien team, we send our sincerest thanks for attending the Summit and for helping us to shape the
future of the C.A.R.E.S. Alliance. We thought it was an incredibly productive discussion and hope you share our enthusiasm for
what we will build together in 2012 and beyond.
Best regards,
Herb Neuman, MD

Subject: Alert: Pharma. Law & Industry Report: Highlights
From: Bloomberg Government <alerts@bgov.com>
Date: Thu, 07 Dec 2017 15:00:34 +0000
To: derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com


{Bloomberg Government}  

 

 

Pharma. Law & Industry Report: Highlights

December 7, 2017 10:00AM ET | Bloomberg BNA


 

 

 

 

HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTENTS

1. Pharma Exec Prosecuted in Off-Label Case Won't Get New Trial

A pharmaceutical company founder's conviction for promoting off-label uses stands, as a federal appeals court found no error in his trial. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

2. Teamsters Health Plan Sues Opioid Manufacturers, Distributors

Opioid manufacturers and distributors are facing yet another suit over their marketing of the painkillers, this time from a Springfield, Mass.-based union health benefit plan. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

3. SCOTUS Seeks Government View in Fosamax Case

The U.S. Supreme Court asked the government Dec. 4 to weigh in on whether it should review a federal appeals court decision reviving some 500 Fosamax product liability suits against Merck & Co. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

4. Opioid Marketing Suits Sent to Federal Court in Ohio

Suits by states and local governments alleging Purdue Pharma LP and other makers of opioid painkillers contributed to an epidemic were sent to federal court in Ohio for consolidated proceedings. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

5. Court Won't Decide Perrigo Prilosec Generic Exclusivity Question

Perrigo Research & Development Co. lost a bid to have a court decide, after the FDA wouldn't, whether it needed to market a generic version of Prilosec now to avoid forfeiting a potentially lucrative exclusivity period. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

6. J&J, Bayer Ordered to Pay $28 Million in First Xarelto Loss

Johnson & Johnson and Bayer AG are responsible for a woman's injuries tied to the blood-thinning drug Xarelto and must pay almost $28 million in damages, jurors concluded in the companies’ first loss at a trial over the medicine. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

7. Compounding Pharmacy Fails to Boot False Claims Lawsuit

A compounding pharmacy the government says deliberately overcharged the federal health-care system for active duty military service members failed to end a lawsuit against it. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

8. Janssen Shielded by Mich. Law Despite Off-Label Risperdal Use

Michigan law immunizes Janssen Pharmaceuticals Inc. from liability in thirteen cases over side effects from the antipsychotic Risperdal, a Pennsylvania appellate court ruled. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

9. Aventis Wins Dismissal in Clomid Birth Defect Suit

Aventis Inc. won dismissal in federal district court of a birth defect suit linked to the prescription fertility drug Clomid. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

10. Opioid Lawyers Warned by Judge Cases Face ‘Serious’ Hurdles

States and local governments suing Purdue Pharma and other makers of opioid painkillers face “serious” legal hurdles that can derail their bids to reap a multibillion-dollar payout to cover the costs of a burgeoning drug epidemic, a federal judge said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

11. Government Should Negotiate Drug Prices, Science Academy Says

The federal government should negotiate drug prices and allow for more flexible drug formularies, a national scientific organization said Nov. 30. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

12. Revisions to Anti-Bribery Law Enforcement Could Prove Significant

Recent revisions to the Justice Department's enforcement policy on the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act could be significant for companies deciding whether to voluntarily disclose wrongdoing under the anti-bribery statute. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

13. FDA Signals Review of Company Executive Liability Approach

The FDA wants to clarify when corporate officers should be held criminally responsible for company wrongdoing, the agency's top lawyer said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

14. Growth of U.S. Health Spending Slows as Drug Prices Decelerate

Total U.S. health spending increased in 2016 but slowed compared with prior years, as Americans shelled out less on prescription drugs and the initial effects of increased Obamacare enrollment dwindled. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

15. FDA Seeks to Speed Approvals of Generic Drug-Device Combos

New FDA guidance will make it easier for generic companies to get drug-device combination products approved. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

16. More Money Needed to Tackle Opioid Crisis, Lawmakers Told

Federal agencies need funding through appropriations to address aspects of the opioid crisis such as research of alternative medication and oversight of insurance company compliance, witnesses said at a hearing on preventing, treating, and recovering from opioid abuse. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

17. States Want Continued Federal Funds to Fight Opioid Epidemic

States are providing more access to addiction treatment and putting more resources into prevention to fight the opioid epidemic, state officials testified before Congress Nov. 30. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

18. Lawmakers Open to New Ideas to Spur Drug, Device Innovation

Members of a key House panel indicated they're open to additional legislative action if necessary to speed new medicines to patients. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

19. Once-Monthly Opioid Addiction Injection Cleared for U.S. Sales

Efforts to combat the opioid epidemic killing thousands of Americans each year got a boost from U.S. regulators with the approval of a first-of-its-kind monthly treatment for addiction to opiates including pills and heroin. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

20. Forget Amazon. Health Companies Really Want to Be UnitedHealth

As the specter of Amazon.com Inc. looms over the health-care industry, it's easy to see the tech giant's threat as a major factor behind the megadeal between CVS Health Corp. and Aetna Inc. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

21. Who's Next? CVS-Aetna Deal Could Start a Health Takeover Run

CVS Health Corp.’s deal to buy insurer Aetna Inc. for about $67.5 billion could be just the start of a new wave of health-care takeovers. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

22. Pharmacy Making Intravenous Drugs Hit With FDA Warning

A New Jersey compounding pharmacy making intravenous drug products received an FDA warning letter for problems that included insanitary manufacturing conditions. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

23. CVS to Buy Aetna for $67.5 Billion, Remaking Health Care Sector

CVS Health Corp. will buy Aetna Inc. for about $67.5 billion, creating a health-care giant that will have a hand in everything from insurance to the corner drugstore. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

24. Newer Birth Control Pills Don't Lower the Risk of Breast Cancer

Newer birth control drugs developed to replace those tied to cancer risk were thought to improve safety for the women who took them. It turns out they didn't, according to a massive new study. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

25. Express Scripts CEO Open to Insurer Deal, Ties with Amazon

Express Scripts Holding Co.’s chief executive said he's open to a deal with a health insurer or partnering with Amazon.com Inc. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

26. U.S. Drug Approval Helps Push Biocon Shares to Fresh Record

Shares of Biocon Ltd. extended a record after U.S. regulators approved its competing version of Roche Holding AG's blockbuster breast cancer drug Herceptin. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

27. Frayed Gasket Delaying Astra's ZS-9 Shows Pharma M&A Perils

When AstraZeneca Plc paid $2.7 billion for an experimental drugmaker in 2015, it had its sights set on a potential blockbuster medicine. Instead, it got a Texas factory riddled with defects and two scathing reviews from U.S. regulators rejecting the treatment. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

28. Biotech Eyes Tax Revamp as Next Chance to Shake Its Recent Woes

Biotechnology investors who saw their portfolios stumble after a late-summer bull run may refocus on a key reason that the group took off: the U.S. tax overhaul and repatriation. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

29. Bayer's Ready to Spend on Its Transformation to Cancer Company

Bayer AG is ready to spend more money on deals and research that will help make it into a cancer company as the company's blockbuster blood-thinner Xarelto nears the final years of its patent life. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

30. CVS Said to Near $65 Billion-Plus Deal for Insurer Aetna

CVS Health Corp. is nearing an agreement to acquire health insurer Aetna Inc. for more than $65 billion, according to a person familiar with the negotiations, in a deal that could reshape the pharmacy and health insurance industries. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

31. A Deadly Drug Cocktail Shines a Light on an AstraZeneca Blockbuster

The last time John Nebinger spoke to his son Bradley was about thirty minutes after midnight on March 15, 2010. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

32. Minnesota Mulls Per-Pill Fee to Counter Opioid Abuse

Pharmaceutical companies would have to pay fees to sell opioids in Minnesota under a bill expected to be introduced in 2018. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

33. This Company Is Ready to Flood the U.S. with Cheap HIV Drugs

Among the coconut plantations and beaches of South India, a factory the size of 35 football fields is preparing to churn out billions of generic pills for HIV patients and flood the U.S. market with the low-cost copycat medicines. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

34. Canada Proposes Tougher Reviews of New Drug Prices

Canada proposed changes to its pricing controls for patented medicines that are projected to lower net drug costs for provincial health plans by C$1.8 billion ($1.2 billion) per year. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

35. Drug Companies from Glaxo to J&J Pledge to Make U.K. Investments

GlaxoSmithKline Plc, Johnson & Johnson, Merck & Co., and AstraZeneca Plc are among more than two dozen global pharmaceutical companies pledging to invest funds in the U.K. as part of a multi-billion-pound effort to spur the country's health-care industry. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

36. European Drug Regulator's Brexit Move Sparks Concern at Genmab

The Brexit-induced relocation of the European medicines regulator to Amsterdam may slow product approvals, hurting some drugmakers, Genmab A/S Chief Executive Officer Jan van de Winkel said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

37. Richter Falls as Liver Cases Prompt Review of Flagship Product

Shares in Gedeon Richter Nyrt., eastern Europe's largest drugmaker, plunged after cases of serious liver injuries prompted the review of one of its flagship products. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

38. 50,000 New Drug Tests Among Brexit Worries for Pharma Companies

Global drugmakers from Johnson & Johnson to AstraZeneca Plc warned that potential trade and regulatory hurdles may burden them with a host of additional costs after Britain leaves the European Union. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

Karen,

Last year (2008) I dispensed 63.5 grams of Codeine Phosphate reference standard for the analytical support of our
manufacturing of the bulk here in St. Louis and all the dosage forms in Hobart. So far this year (2009) I have dispensed 13


   grams. Last year Sherryl Ruder shipped one order for 200 milligrams to an external customer and had no internal requests for
Codeine Phosphate.

If I were to subdivide 1000 grams, that would last us almost 16 years at the rate that we used it in 2008. I must say that our
reference standard use is increasing, so that 1000 grams may only last maybe 10 years. That still is a very long time to store a
qualified reference. I also know that storing any controlled substance that long invites opportunities for diversion. So that
generally should be discouraged.

We use the manufacturing registration for our operation. When it is shipped to Hobart  it goes out under our manufacturing
registration and is transferred to Hobart's Analytical registration via their form 222.

It seems to me that if the customer is "manufacturing" a reference standard, it should be received into their manufacturing
registration. When it goes to their client to be used in the lab, that is when it should be transferred to analytical lab registration.

Ted

registration for the work you do in "making" ARS compounds, customer is requesting the material on an Analytical Lab DEA

Our regulatory interpretation is that use of Analytical Lab DEA registration is reserved for an entity that actually performs tests

February 4, 2014
Poster Presentation Notification
We are pleased to inform you that your abstract entitled "Assessment Of
Adverse Events After MNK-795 (Oxycodone And Acetaminophen ExtendedRelease Tablets) In Healthy Adult Volunteers" has been accepted for
presentation in a poster session at the 2014 Annual Meeting, World Congress
on Exercise is Medicine, and World Congress on the Role of Inflammation in
Exercise, Health and Disease of the American College of Sports Medicine being

MNKOI 0004000479

 held at the Orange County Convention Center in Orlando, Florida, May 27- 31,
2014. Your abstract will be published in Medicine and Science in Sports and
Exercise, Volume 46:5 Supplement. Your presentation date and time are as
follows:
Name:
Srinivas Nalamachu
Session Viewing Date/Time: Friday May 30, 2014 1:00 PM - 6:00 PM
Session Number:
F-30
Presentation Time:
2:00pm - 3:30pm
Session Details
Attendees consider the poster sessions an important and valuable part of the
educational program of the Annual Meeting, World Congress on Exercise is
Medicine, and World Congress on the Role of Inflammation in Exercise, Health
and Disease. Therefore, the Program Committee has extended the viewing
times of the posters. If you are presenting your poster in a morning session,
you must mount your poster on the assigned display board at 7:30 a.m. and
remove your material at 12:30 p.m. (If presenting on Saturday, you will need
to remove your material at 11:00 a.m.) If you are presenting your poster in an
afternoon session, you must mount your poster on the assigned display board
at 1:00 p.m. and remove your material at 6:00 p.m. You are required to be
present at your poster during the entire one and one-half hour presentation
time, which is listed above. Your poster must be mounted for the entire viewing
time as listed above.
Because of the importance of the poster sessions, we have a policy that applies
to those infrequent instances when a session does not occur as scheduled. We
note there have been several "no shows" among posters over the last few
years, which disappoints attendees and detracts from the program. To address
this, and maintain the quality and dependability of the program, the Program
Committee now has assigned a chairperson to oversee the poster sessions. The
chairperson will monitor that posters are placed on boards as assigned and that
the author is present at the poster during the designated time.
Failure to present is considered a no-show and the Program Committee will
contact you following the meeting for an explanation. The Board of Trustees
has a long-standing policy stating that speakers who fail to provide notice of a
reason acceptable to the Program Committee for not delivering an accepted
paper will be prohibited from presenting at future Annual Meetings. Also, be
advised per Program Committee policy, only the first author may withdraw the
abstract.
In the event an emergency arises prior to or during the meeting that prohibits
you from presenting your material, please immediately inform Danielle Davis in
the Education Department at ACSM in writing by e-mailing ddavis@acsm.org.

Format" and follow the "Instructions for Poster Presentations ..." Click here for

among the concurrent sessions at the meeting. As I am sure you will appreciate,
it is quite an undertaking to create a meeting program without overlapping

consider any change requests related to the date and time of sessions. We

Photography and videotaping are not allowed in any scientific or clinical
session. Please refrain from taking photos during this session.

April 23, 2014. (NOTE: should you pre-register by March 19, you can take

allows ACSM the opportunity to ensure all speakers have registered for the

room through ACSM's housing bureau will ensure you are in the center of the
action. Make plans early for a better chance at your preferred hotel! For
housing details and to reserve your hotel room, Click here.

arrangements, please contact ACSM's preferred travel agency, ALTOUR. Call

Thank you for your contribution to the program - we look forward to your
presentation.

The other day you had sent me a note that asked about the status of our Fentanyl Lozenge in regards to our Fentanyl Lozenge being unmatched on CMS.   I just received the e mail information below which highlights and confirms that our Fentanyl Lozenge is listed on the FDA website.   With our Lozenge being listed, it also highlights that the non match list will be updated, and our Lozenge will be removed from the unmatched list.

CMS utilizes FDA's NDC website (http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/ndc/default.cfm) to determine whether a product should be listed as a Non-Matched product.  The Fentanyl Lozenge was not listed on the FDA's NDC website and was therefore listed as a Non-Match product.  Our regulatory team addressed the issue and as of yesterday, the Fentanyl Lozenge is now listed on the NDC website.  According to our reimbursement group, CMS expects to update the list one time in December 2010 with deletions for new listings on the FDA NDC Directory since October 2010.  We will use the updated December list to establish new edits beginning on or around January 1, 2011 that will reject prescription drug event (PDE) submissions from Part D sponsors for NDCs identified.  Additionally, our reimbursement group is contacting CMS directly with documentation that reflects the Fentanyl Lozenge being listed on the NDC website.

Subject: Alert: Health Care Policy Report: Highlights
From: Bloomberg Government <alerts@bgov.com>
Date: Fri, 13 Oct 2017 16:15:53 +0000
To: derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com


{Bloomberg Government}  

 

 

Health Care Policy Report: Highlights

October 13, 2017 12:15PM ET | Bloomberg BNA


 

 

 

 

The following is the latest issue of the Bloomberg BNA Health Care Policy Reports:

HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTENTS

1. Trump Threatens Obamacare Chaos as He Cuts Off Insurer Subsidy

President Donald Trump's administration took its most drastic step yet to roll back the Affordable Care Act on the evening of Oct. 12, cutting off a subsidy to insurers just hours after issuing an executive order designed to draw people away from the health law's coverage markets. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

2. Democrats Skeptical of New Children's Health Deal

Republicans aren't willing to change significant details of their bill extending funding for the Children's Health Insurance Program, which is likely to kill chances Democrats will support it, Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.) told Bloomberg BNA Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

3. Trump Moves to Undo Obamacare After Repeal Drive Fails on Hill

President Donald Trump began his own effort to undo major parts of the Affordable Care Act, after Republican leaders in Congress failed to repeal and replace his predecessor's signature legislative accomplishment. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

4. GOP Lawmaker Calls for Transparency in Drug Discount Program

Congress must ensure accountability and transparency in the federal 340B drug discount program, Rep. Morgan Griffith (R-Va.) said Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

5. Trump Cuts to Obamacare Enrollment Groups Deeper Than Expected

The Trump administration is cutting tens of millions of dollars from organizations that help Americans enroll in Obamacare health plans, leaving some of the groups scrambling to shrink their operations weeks before enrollment for 2018 coverage opens on Nov. 1. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

6. Democrats Seek Relaxed Medicaid Rules for Hurricane Victims

Federal authorities should relax Medicaid eligibility rules for those affected by hurricanes in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, House Democrats told the Trump administration. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

7. Puerto Rico Medicaid Funding in Spotlight After Hurricane

The House Energy and Commerce Committee passed in a divided vote $1 billion in additional funding for Puerto Rico's Medicaid program as part of its bill reauthorizing the lapsed Children's Health Insurance Program. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

8. House Approves Federal Diabetes Panel

Health officials would create a new panel to coordinate the federal response to diabetes and related illnesses under a bill passed by the House Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

9. What GOP Budget Means for Health Care

Republicans say they'll keep their tax reform and Obamacare overhaul plans separate, but Democrats are warning that the GOP left the door open for changes to the health law as well as to Medicare and Medicaid. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

10. Groups, States Oppose HHS Change to Birth Control Mandate

Opposition to Trump administration changes to rules implementing Obamacare's birth control coverage requirement is moving into court. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

11. Many Ideas, Little Consensus in House on Opioid Epidemic

There appears to be little consensus among House lawmakers about how Congress should respond to the opioid epidemic. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

12. Trump Names Hargan as Acting Health and Human Services Secretary

President Donald Trump has formally designated Eric Hargan as acting secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, taking over for a deputy who's held the job since Tom Price resigned from the post late last month over his use of taxpayer dollars to travel in private jets. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

13. Trump Slows Efforts to Cut Health-Care Costs

In April 2016 the federal Medicare program began an experiment to save money on the half-million hip and knee replacements it pays for each year. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

14. Obamacare Would Be Further Weakened by Trump Order, Experts Say

An executive order from President Donald Trump to allow new health plans outside of Obamacare could further destabilize the law's fragile markets, health-care experts say. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

15. Almost Half of Medicare Managed Care Plans Get Top Ratings

Close to half (44 percent) of Medicare managed care plans that combine health services and the Part D drug benefit are rated at least four stars on a one-to-five scale for the 2018 plan year, the Medicare agency said Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

16. Medicare Panel Wants Congress to Scrap Doctor Reporting Program

Congress's Medicare advisers Oct. 5 appeared close to recommending that the nine-month-old physician quality reporting system be killed. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

17. Extend Relaxed Medicare Doc Pay Rules, Groups Tell Congress

Congress should allow Medicare to continue slowing down implementation of certain provisions of the new doctor quality payment program for three more years, the American Medical Association and 114 medical groups said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

18. Medicare Panel Urges Caution on Telehealth Expansion

Congress's Medicare advisers are concerned it may be premature to expand telehealth coverage. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

19. GOP Senators Push for Vote on 20-Week Abortion Ban

Several Senate Republicans Oct. 5 called for a vote on a House-passed ban on abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

20. Senator Demands OPM Explain Treatment of Congress Under ACA

The Office of Personnel Management is being asked to produce, by Oct. 18, all of the information it has regarding the Obama-era decision to allow members of Congress and their staffs to get special consideration, including an employer contribution, for their health plans under the Affordable Care Act. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

21. Trump Order on Health Insurance Sales Across State Lines Delayed

An executive order from President Donald Trump boosting sales of health insurance across state lines has been delayed, according to people following the issue. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

22. California Laws Protect Obamacare from Federal Threats

Gov. Jerry Brown (D) signed bills Oct. 4 to prop up California's embrace of the Affordable Care Act in the face of federal changes. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

23. Federal Subsidy Uncertainty Means Calif. Obamacare Hike

California's health benefits exchange is tacking an average 12.4 percent surcharge on some plans in 2018 to minimize the uncertainty of federal cost-sharing subsidies from the Trump administration. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

24. Nevada Legislature Intervenes in Drug-Pricing Lawsuit

The Nevada Legislature is stepping in to defend a new drug-pricing law that industry groups say violates the U.S. Constitution. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

25. Will Storm-Struck Nursing Home Find Shelter From Litigation?

Families suing a Florida nursing home over its post-hurricane evacuation and more than a dozen deaths will have to work around state laws that attorneys say shelter the industry from large damages awards. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

26. Planned Parenthood, ACLU Team Up to Take on Missouri Abortion Law

A Missouri law set to take effect Oct. 24 that places additional restrictions on legal abortion is invalid, two abortion rights groups claim. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

27. Pennsylvania Joins States With Drug, Device Right-to-Try Laws

Terminally ill patients in Pennsylvania will have the right to try experimental treatments under legislation Gov. Tom Wolf (D) signed into law Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

28. West Virginia to Use Medicaid for Substance Abuse Treatment

West Virginia, which has the highest rate of drug overdose deaths in the country, will become the fifth state to use Medicaid dollars to battle substance abuse. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

29. Union Alleges Seattle-Area Health System Fails Charity Duty

An organized-labor backed report released Oct. 10 accuses CHI Franciscan Health, a metropolitan Seattle health-care system, of failing to follow its legal and moral obligations to provide charity care. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

30. Tennessee Doctors Say Payment Reform Effort Flawed

Tennessee's episodes-of-care incentive payment program is flawed and unfair and not working for physicians, a representative of state providers says. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

31. Physicians Leading Campaign for Alaska Insurance Provisions

A group of Alaska doctors is offering two ballot initiatives that would establish several popular features of the Affordable Care Act as statewide insurance requirements. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

32. Drug Profits Catch Wall Street's Eye in Flurry of FDA Approvals

Gridlock under the Trump administration, particularly the repeated failures to repeal and replace Obamacare, is riveting the nation's attention. Yet at least one government agency is running smoothly—and even accelerating its operations. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

33. Drugmakers Face Puerto Rico Factory Challenges as Storm Passes

Drugmakers rode out Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, but keeping plants running while the devastated island picks up the pieces is likely to be tougher. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

34. Express Scripts to Buy Medical Gatekeeper for $3.6 Billion

Express Scripts Holding Co. agreed to pay $3.6 billion to acquire closely held EviCore Healthcare, a company that preapproves scans and other costly medical tests for health plans. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

35. Amazon Looms Over Pharmacy Chains as Analysts See Market Entry

Amazon.com Inc. is almost certain to enter the business of selling prescription drugs by 2019, said two analysts at Leerink Partners, posing a direct threat to the U.S.’s biggest brick-and-mortar drugstore chains. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

36. Disaster Preparedness Essentials for Healthcare Facilities

Natural disasters cause nearly 500 deaths annually in the United States. Unfortunately, healthcare facilities in the U.S. continue to fall short in disaster planning and preparedness. This lack of preparation creates the potential for serious ramifications, putting staff, patients, and the financial security of the hospital at risk. Contact: DOH Office of Communications
(850) 245-4111

FIVE MIAMI PHARMACIES ORDERED TO STOP OPERATING
 - Two year multi-agency investigation identifies pill mill scam -


TALLAHASSEE   The Florida Department of Health (DOH) today suspended five pharmacy permits, immediately ordering the pharmacies and the entire staff to cease operations, based on investigative findings in partnership with the United States Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) that the pharmacy owner and its pharmacists dispensed controlled substances, other than in the course of the professional practice of pharmacy.

 Florida s law enforcement and public health leaders remain committed to our ongoing effort to end the criminal distribution of prescription drugs, and I thank them for their great work,  said Governor Rick Scott.   Removing the sources of these drugs is essential to saving lives and stopping this scourge on our communities.

Four of the five Miami pharmacies are owned by Aiman Aryan, a licensed pharmacist. The pharmacies operate under the business name of Robert s Drug Store and are responsible for purchasing more than 1.6 million pills of oxycodone-based medications starting January 1 through June 30, 2011.

 The severity of this epidemic cannot be overstated,  said Dr. Farmer.  DOH is committed to suspending and revoking the licenses of unscrupulous practitioners and pharmacies who inappropriately prescribe highly addictive controlled substances to patients, with the hopes of stopping countless senseless deaths in our state.

Further investigative efforts revealed that the pharmacies had  recruiters  who would pick up Medicare  patients  and drive them various doctor s offices who would write a prescription to the patient for a controlled substance without a legitimate medical purpose and without performing a physical examination of the patient. After obtaining the prescription, the patient was transported to one of the four Robert s Drug Stores to have the prescription filled.  The recruiters paid the patients $600 for their medications that usually consisted of 720 pills per patient. When the prescription was brought to one of the Robert s Drug Stores, Mr. Aryan would pay the recruiters in cash for bringing patients to his pharmacies to have prescriptions filled.

The four pharmacies owned by Aryan also worked under the business names of Pharmacy One Inc. and Izz & Sons, Inc.

At the same time today, Pharmalife Consultant Inc., was also issued an emergency suspension order mandating the pharmacy permit be suspending after an investigation revealed that the pharmacy filled over 150 fraudulent prescriptions accounting for 23,500 oxycodone pills.

The ESOs were issued as a result of investigative assistance provided by the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA), US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), United States Attorney s Office, Miami-Dade Police Department and the Broward County Sheriff s Office.


View the complete Order listed above on DOH s Online Newsroom at http://newsroom.doh.state.fl.us/category/healthcare-licensing/ <http://newsroom.doh.state.fl.us/category/healthcare-licensing/> .

Emergency suspension or restriction orders are not considered final agency action but are imposed as specified by section 456.074, Florida Statutes, for serious violations relating to the commission of crimes, standard of care, drug use, or for student loan defaults. The subject is entitled to a hearing before final action is taken by a regulatory board or by DOH.

To learn more about the Florida Department of Health visit www.doh.state.fl.us <http://www.doh.state.fl.us> .

###

The mission of the Florida Department of Health and Medical Quality Assurance (MQA) is to protect and promote the health of all residents and visitors in the state through organized state and community efforts, including cooperative agreements with counties. Working in conjunction with 22 boards and six councils, MQA regulates six types of facilities and more than 40 healthcare professions. MQA evaluates the credentials of all applicants for licensure, issues licenses, analyzes and investigates complaints, inspects facilities, assists in prosecuting practice act violations, combats unlicensed activity and provides credential and discipline history about licensees to the public.

Subject: Couple of Discussion Topics - Deck of Truth notes Obstacles/Barriers & COVIDIEN/GSW 360 evaluation tool
From: "Gunn, Edward" <egunn@gsw-w.com>
Date: Fri, 01 Apr 2011 12:45:49 -0500
To: "wessler, michael"


When: Monday, April 04, 2011 10:00 AM-10:30 AM (GMT-05:00) Eastern Time (US & Canada).
Where: TBD - teleconference 
 
Note: The GMT offset above does not reflect daylight saving time adjustments.
 
*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*
 
I ll call you, Mike.
 
Mike:
 
It was really good to see you yesterday.  I know you have a lot going on but I am requesting about 30 minutes of your time to discuss the following topics:
 
          Deck of Truth   follow up (Obstacles/Barriers below)
          CRM   COVIDIEN/GSW 360 evaluation tool   (Attached is a draft tool in development) 
o   Review 
   Joint effort between GSW NY & C
   Draft at starting point
   Corporate behaviors   GSW & COVIDIEN   how the tool could potentially support both needs
   Timing of team feedback from COVIDIEN
 
Deck of Truth Obstacles/Barriers Discussion
 
Below is the list of Barriers/Obstacles that were discussed at the end of our meeting.  Please insure that I have captured them correctly, and if not, make any adjustments necessary. I have taken a stab at placing them in order of EXALGO success priority, but as discussed, we will need for your team to confirm.  Ultimately we can put 2-3 obstacles/barriers into our inVentiv network now.  Others we are happy to put through a little later.
 
          Limited Sales Training Support
o   Presently within COVIDIEN, Sales Training is a shared service.  This has resulted in an internal brand weakness for EXALGO due to a physical lack of resources for the branded personal sales organization. inVentiv Health support will focus on the advancement of field force training -  for new and experienced sales representatives.
          Effective Conversion & Titration to EXALGO
o   When converting patients from an existing opioid product to EXALGO, the labeling currently directs HCPs to sum the total daily dose of the patient s existing opioid and multiple that dose by listed conversion ratios to calculate the approximate oral hydromorphone equivalent.  The labeling then directs, in general terms, that the HCP should administer 50% of the calculated total daily dose of EXALGO every 24 hours. The initial dose of EXALGO can then be titrated to adequate pain relief with tolerable side effects.  The direction of administration of 50% of the dose for EXALGO is resulting in patients  pain being under-treated, or in some cases opioid withdrawal due to physician inexperience with conversion of these type of opioids, especially in those patients on a large dose of their existing opioid.  InVentiv Health partners will look to give guidance on how to better communicate the conversion to EXALGO in various communication channels.
          Repositioning hydromorphone
o   A significant strategy for EXALGO.  Most HCPs have a current perception of hydromorphone through experience with IR hydromorphone (q4-6hr), or Dilaudid. Historically IR hydromorphone has been seen as a very effective pain reliever but also highly abused/diverted in its oral formulation.  An internal brand weakness for EXALGO is physicians  feeling that because of the strength, potency, and abuse potential of hydormorphone, EXALGO should be used significantly later in their treatment algorithm. InVentiv Health partners will look to give guidance on how to better communicate the effectiveness and safety of once-daily EXALGO while allaying concerns surrounding abuse in various communication channels.
          Identify the EXALGO patient
o   EXALGO is indicated for use in only opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time. The indication is very broad and theoretically, any opioid tolerant chronic pain patient is a candidate for EXALGO.  Since several ER opioid analgesic products have been on the market before EXALGO, we know that HCPs have established prescribing habits of 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc. line products that they are comfortable using. In this type of situation, the brand needs to identify the patient profile that offers the best opportunity, or scenario, for which EXALGO would be an optimal choice of treatment. InVentiv Health partners will help identify the types of patient profiles Best suited for successful conversion to EXALGO.
          EXALGO   New 32mg strength launch (Coverage/Pricing)
o   Because EXALGO was limited to 8, 12, and 16 mg strengths, the lack of a higher strength dose has left the brand at a disadvantage when patients are converted from their existing higher dose opioid to EXALGO.  Patients are having to take multiple dosage strengths to get to the optimal daily dose.  With current monthly limitations on CII opioids this creates hassles for physicians and patients. The addition of a 32 mg strength will help reduce the number of EXALGO pills a patient will need to consume once-daily. It will also offer the brand the opportunity to adjust their pricing strategy. InVentiv Health partners will investigate launch strategies for the 32 mg dose, and pricing strategies for the existing line of dosage strengths to optimize managed care coverage.
 
When you have the opportunity, please let me know when would be a good time to chat on Friday, 4/1, or Monday, 4/4.
 
Best,
 
Ed

  pain when a continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extensive period. 

  The post-marketing studies are intended to be epidemiological or observational trials to assess the drugs' known 
  serious risks as well as whether their abuse deterrent properties "actually result in a decrease" of abuse and 
  misuse as well as curtailing their potential consequences - addiction, overdose and death, according to FDA. 

  FDA is happy to see the development of potentially safer opioids, but the agency has been loathe to give the 
  products a claim for abuse deterrence, since simply engineering the pills not to be enjoyed doesn't prove they 
  will work that way, and a controlled trial couldn't ethically have misuse as a endpoint. 

  The advisory committee meeting, set for Oct. 21 and Oct. 22 in Gaithersburg, Md., is a signal, though, that the 
  agency may consider allowing different kinds of data to support risk reduction language in the label. 

  Getting The Message Out With A REMS 
  Having an abuse reduction claim or even just robust data in labeling would be a great benefit for either product, 
  particularly as the agency may be pushing all sponsors to shift their promotional efforts to a risk and education 
  message as part of a potential class-wide Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy for long-acting and extended- 
  release opioids. 

  In July, the agency issued a proposed REMS for long-acting opioids, to consist of a MedGuide, requirements 
  for drug sponsors to provide prescriber education, requirements for educational sheets to be offered to patients, 
  and a program and timetable for assessing the plan's effectiveness ('FDA's Guide To Mitigating Risks Of Long- 
  Acting Opioids,' The Pink Sheet, July 5, 2010). 

  But the Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs and Drug Safety and Risk Management advisory committees voted 
  against approval of the FDA proposal by 10-25 on July 22. Panel members cited concerns that prescriber 
  participation in the educational programs would be voluntary rather than mandatory. 

  The panel also considered an industry proposal for an opioids REMS during that meeting, suggesting that if 
  prescriber education be mandatory, implementation be through either a third-party industry-wide registry or a 
  Drug Enforcement Administration registry that would require approval by Congress. Industry participants 
  indicated they probably would prefer the latter option ('If Opioid REMS Mandates Prescriber Training, Firms 
  May Ask DEA For Help,' The Pink Sheet, Aug. 2, 2010).

Press Release

 
 
 

MCKESSON AGREES TO PAY RECORD $150 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS

 

JAN 17 - (Washington, DC) – McKesson Corporation (McKesson), one of the nation’s largest distributors of pharmaceutical drugs, agreed to pay a record $150 million civil penalty for alleged violations of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.

 

The nationwide settlement requires McKesson to suspend sales of controlled substances from distribution centers in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida for multiple years. The staged suspensions are among the most severe sanctions ever agreed to by a DEA-registered distributor. The settlement also imposes new and enhanced compliance obligations on McKesson’s distribution system.

 

In 2008, McKesson agreed to a $13.25 million civil penalty and administrative agreement for similar violations. In this case, the government alleged again that McKesson failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report “suspicious orders” for controlled substances distributed to its independent and small chain pharmacy customers– i.e. orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2013, McKesson supplied various U.S. pharmacies an increasing amount of oxycodone and hydrocodone pills, frequently misused products that are part of the current opioid epidemic.

 

The government’s investigation developed evidence that even after designing a compliance program after the 2008 settlement, McKesson did not fully implement or adhere to its own program. In Colorado, for example, McKesson processed more than 1.6 million orders for controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but reported just 16 orders as suspicious, all connected to one instance related to a recently terminated customer. 

 

"This groundbreaking resolution is tough and appropriate and underscores our commitment to hold accountable all DEA registrants, including those who distribute controlled substances," said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  "DEA is committed to fighting the opioid epidemic with all of the tools at our disposal."

 

In addition to the monetary penalties and suspensions, the government and McKesson agreed to enhanced compliance terms for the next five years. Among other things, McKesson has agreed to specific, rigorous staffing and organizational improvements; periodic auditing; and stipulated financial penalties for failing to adhere to the compliance terms. Critically, the settlement will require McKesson to engage an independent monitor to assess compliance – the first independent monitor of its kind in a CSA civil penalty settlement.

 

This was a multi-district investigation that involved the following DEA Field Divisions:  Boston Field Division, Chicago Field Division, Denver Field Division, Detroit Field Division, Miami Field Division, New Jersey Field Division, San Francisco Field Division, St. Louis Field Division, and Washington Division Office. The following U.S. Attorneys’ Offices participated in the case: Central District of California, Eastern District of California, District of Colorado, Middle District of Florida, Eastern District of Kentucky, Northern District of Illinois, District of Massachusetts, Eastern District of Michigan, District of Nebraska, District of New Jersey, Northern District of West Virginia, and Western District of Wisconsin.

 

U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the District of Colorado and the Northern District of West Virginia, along with DEA’s Office of Chief Counsel and its Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations.  DEA’s Denver, Detroit and Miami Field Divisions and its Washington Division Office led the administrative and civil investigation. The U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating certain portions of the settlement. Assistant United States Attorneys Amanda Rocque (Colorado) and Alan McGonigal (NDWV) represented the United States in the civil penalty investigations and negotiations.  Associate Chief Counsel Lee Reeves and Senior Attorneys Dedra Curteman, Dana Hill and Krista Tongring represented DEA in the investigations and negotiations. Trial Attorneys Harry Matz and Kirtland Marsh were involved for NDDS.

From: Patrick, Jeffrey

To: Wickline, Ronald P; Novak, Rod P
Cc: Neuman, Herbert R; Meyer, Jay E; McGowan, Gavin J; Kisinger, Connie ; Wessler, Michael
Subject: FW: Label Language - Converting to Exalgo



Sales and Marketing Colleagues,

 

Please see the email I sent to Herb following a discussion we had on potential educational needs for physicians on issues surrounding the conversion process of patients on other opioids to Exalgo. The Exalgo label excerpts that I included below provide treating physicians with information that is pertinent to the management of the opioid rotation process to Exalgo, however, there are questions regarding physicians awareness of these additional elements of the label, as they are located somewhat deeper in the label and there is likelihood that physicians may not have thoroughly read these elements as a result.

 

We believe that some, if not many, physicians may be utilizing only part of the conversion recommendations (the general recommendation for dose reduction of 50%) and they may not necessarily be implementing other elements as described in the label to ensure the process is managed thoroughly and safely. There may be educational needs for the physicians on the aspect of the opiate deficit that is created by the employing the recommended dose reduction which can lead to withdrawal symptoms, which is why it may be important to utilize other steps that are described in the label language, such as monitoring rescue medication usage. Additionally, the importance of understanding the pharmacokinetics of Exalgo is pertinent to the conversion and titration aspect, which may result in the requirement of supportive rescue medication and physician evaluation of patients  response and side effects, until the patient is at steady-state on Exalgo. Finally, as the label language suggests, there is no single fixed conversion ratio that will suitably address the needs of all patients and physicians might benefit by being apprised of alternative conversion options, such as that employed in the pivotal 301 study published by Hale et al, which utilized a 25% dose reduction and the proceeded with titration.  

 

An idea we had was to consider developing a leave-behind educational card, with  Considerations for Conversion to Exalgo  that would utilize the label language elements on conversion and titration (such as those included below) and provide physicians with a succinct review of the FDA recommendations for the process of conversion to and titration of Exalgo. However, if the sales force already cover these elements or have an educational piece of this nature, there is no need to be redundant.

 

We look forward to your thoughts and input on this subject.

 

Thank you.

 

jtp

 

From: Patrick, Jeffrey
Sent: Wednesday, December 08, 2010 6:38 PM
To: Neuman, Herbert R
Cc: Patrick, Jeffrey
Subject: Label Language - Converting to Exalgo



 

Herb,


 


Appropriately, the FDA wrote the label language to aid and direct physicians in their efforts to convert patients to Exalgo. However, they did not suggest that there is one fixed process that will satisfy all patients converted. The following EXALGO label excerpts point to the need for the prescribing physician to utilize their clinical judgement as well as close communication to best manage patients in the conversion process:


 


In the selection of the initial dose of EXALGO, give attention to the following:

? the daily dose, potency, and specific characteristics of the opioid the patient has been taking previously;

? the reliability of the relative potency estimate used to calculate the equivalent hydromorphone dose needed;

? the patient's degree of opioid tolerance;

? the age, general condition, and medical status of the patient;

? concurrent non-opioid analgesics and other medications, such as those with Central Nervous System (CNS) activity [see Drug Interactions (7)];

? the type and severity of the patient's pain;

? the balance between pain control and adverse effects;

? risk factors for abuse, addiction, or diversion, including a prior history of abuse, addiction, or diversion

 

In general, start EXALGO therapy by administering 50% of the calculated total daily dose of EXALGO (see conversion ratio table below) every 24 hours. The initial dose of EXALGO can be titrated until adequate pain relief with  tolerable side effects has been achieved. The following table provides approximate equivalent doses, which may be used as a guideline for conversion.

? The conversion ratios and approximate equivalent doses in this conversion table (Table 1) are only to be used for the conversion from current oral opioid therapy to EXALGO. No fixed conversion ratio is likely to be satisfactory in all patients, especially in patients receiving large opioid doses.

Individualization of Dosage

? Once therapy is initiated, assess pain relief and other opioid adverse reactions frequently.

? Titrate patients to adequate analgesia with dose increases not more often than every 3 to 4 days, in order to attain steady-state plasma concentrations of hydromorphone at each dose.

? As a guideline, consider dosage increases of 25% to 50% of the current daily dose of EXALGO for each titration step.

? If more than two doses of rescue medication are needed within a 24 hour period for two consecutive days, the dose of EXALGO may need to be titrated upward.

? Administer EXALGO no more frequently than every 24 hours.

During periods of changing analgesic requirements, including initial titration, maintain frequent contact between physician, other members of the healthcare team, the patient and the caregiver/family.

 

I believe these are educational points for all discussions related to patients who have Exalgo prescribed for them.

 

jtp

DEA Compliance Procedure   No:
Subject:  Revision  No.:
 1
Controlled Substance Suspicious Order Monitoring  Effective Date:

 Supersedes Date:
NEW
 Page No.:
1  of 3

Originator: Security:
Karen Harper
Corporate Logistics: Documentation Coordinator:


PURPOSE:
Establish a procedure to identify and report controlled substance suspicious orders  to the Drug
Enforcement Administration
SCOPE:
Applies to establishing a new controlled substance customer account and subsequent shipment of
all controlled substance orders to new or established customers.
REFERENCES:
Title 21 CFR 1301.74(b)
The registrant shall design and operate a system to disclose to the registrant suspicious orders of
controlled substances. The registrant shall inform the Field Division Office of the Administration
in his area of suspicious orders when discovered by the registrant. Suspicious  orders include
orders of unusual size, orders deviating substantially from a normal pattern, and orders of
unusual frequency..
DEFINITIONS:
Peculiar Order   A controlled substance order that meets and internal, established criteria
that will be placed on  hold  pending further review by DEA Compliance.
Suspicious Order  A controlled substance Peculiar Order that has been reviewed by DEA
Compliance and Security that will not be shipped and will be reported to
the Drug Enforcement Administration.


   QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  2  of 3


RESPONSIBILITIES:
Credit Department or Customer Data Integrity Group
Perform Dun & Bradstreet information check on new controlled substance customers to
determine credit worthiness.
Refer  the new customer account to Security Director or DEA Compliance if the new account has
no historical or financial information available or if the data shows liens, lawsuits, or other
information which might raise suspicions as to the legitimacy  of the new account company.
Conduct periodic checks on our  existing customers if they ve been put on credit hold two times
in the previous 12 months.
Field Sales
Completes Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers (Attachment A)
Customer Service Representative
Completes Controlled Substance Order Checklist (Attachment B) and refers orders that meet the
Peculiar Order criteria to DEA Compliance and Security Director for review
Customer Service Manager
Obtains a daily report from the order entry system that highlights orders deviating in qua ntity
from an established order pattern calculation to determine if order quantity fits Peculiar Order
criteria and refers to DEA Compliance and Security Director for review
Security Director
Provides Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers to be completed by
Field Sales
Reviews results of Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers and provides
authorization to proceed with new customer account set-up
In conjunction with DEA Compliance, reviews controlled substance or ders that have been
identified as Peculiar Orders by Customer Service and makes the ship or do not ship decision
Reports orders deemed Suspicious to the Drug Enforcement Administration
DEA Compliance
Provides updated  Drugs of Concern  listing to Customer  Service quarterly
Provides Controlled Substance Order Checklist to Customer Service


  QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  3  of 3

In conjunction with Security Director, reviews controlled substance orders that have been
identified as Peculiar Orders by Customer Service and makes the ship or do not ship decision
Reports orders deemed Suspicious to the Drug Enforcement Administration.
Maintains a file at the St. Louis Plant Site for record retention of Suspicious Order Monitoring
documents and reports.

{e-Pharm/alert } 
{e-Pharm/alert  Providing important information to healthcare professionals since 1976} {e-Pharm/alert } 
{e-Pharm/alert } 



Why stock the 32 mg tablet?

 

 EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*1

 
 

 You may already be distributing multiple 16 mg tablets to patients.

 
*

 Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.2

 

EXALGO TABLET STRENGTHS2

Tablets shown are not actual size.

START STOCKING EXALGO 32 MG TODAY!

REFERENCES: 1. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518.
2. EXALGO  Prescribing Information.

800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally
registered trademarks of Covidien AG.
EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20164 September 2012

To ensure that you receive future email from EXALGO, add us to your address book.
If you no longer wish to receive email from EXALGO, unsubscribe now.

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications

Danielle

As you requested, I have made modifications to slides 17, 19 and 20 and since I cannot mark through items, I have entered several comments where needed. On slide 17 & 19, I modified the tables based on the groupings described below. I also added the source as the following on slides 17 & 19: Mallinckrodt Post-marketing Safety Database. On slide 19, please delete the following: Most events included multiple medications. On slide 20, please delete the word serious as well as Events are not necessarily related to EXALGO/JURNISTA.

I realize the initial data provided to you was quite detailed by very specific events. I have now grouped events accordingly which will likely be more meaningful for your needs and this slide deck. The specific events that were listed fall in to categories for the REMS reports of interest and I am explaining how I have updated the tables in the PowerPoint below.

For Jurnista with a total of 40 events:

          Medication errors (includes Drug prescribing error, Inappropriate schedule of drug administration, Wrong technique in drug usage process, Incorrect dose administered, Drug label confusion, and Medication error) for a total of 14

          Abuse or misuse (includes Drug abuse, Drug dependence, Intentional drug misuse, Drug diversion and Product Tampering) for a total of 11

          Overdose (includes Overdose, Multiple drug overdose, Multiple drug overdose intentional, and Intentional overdose) for a total of 10

          Suicide attempt remains listed with 3

          Accidental drug intake by child remains listed with 2

For Exalgo with a total of 22 events (I am suggesting to remove 1 event of Toxicity to various agents as this does not fall under the REMS reports of interest):

          Medication errors (includes Inappropriate schedule of drug administration, Drug prescribing error, Medication error and Incorrect dose administered) for a total of 9

          Abuse or misuse (includes Intentional drug misuse, Product tampering and Substance abuse) for a total of 6

          Overdose (includes Accidental overdose, Overdose, Intentional overdose) for a total of 5

          Completed suicide remains listed with 1

          Suicide attempt remains listed with 1

Should you need anything additional from me, please let me know.

Best Regards,
Danielle
